***

For twenty years, I have lived within half a mile of it. I can pinpoint its location to the west, marked by the black iron weather-hen—half-strangled by clematis—atop the garage roof. Past a low ridge along the cliff face of a limestone dale, a cave lies concealed within the bushes. 

Long after the ancient tigers had vanished, leaving only their teeth behind, the valley people would ascend to this spot bearing the deceased they deemed most vital. They would place them deep inside, retrieve them later, and parade them about, calling out, “They’re coming! They’re coming!” 

We Malagasy people cherish our tradition of second burials; we hire a band that arrives in a van. Once decomposition is nearly complete, we hold our cherished departed in our arms once more. From their grave-shrouds, fragments slip free in heavy gobbets, much like pet food sliding from a can. We rewrap them in fresh, dry linen, and they bless our lives with their happiness as we walk them through the valley. Here, we leave a finger as an offering to a deity embodied by a rat or a raven; there, we place a metatarsal beneath the hearth for good fortune. 

And what was luck? The afterlife in those days was reasonably long—neither unnaturally infinite nor rigidly regimented. It was an afterlife that would actively join the celebration.

***

For two decades, my home has been situated less than half a mile from this spot. Its position can be pinpointed by looking west toward a garage, where a black iron hen-shaped weather vane—choked by climbing clematis—sits on the roof. Just past a low ledge on the rocky wall of a limestone valley, a cavern hides among the bushes. 

Ages after prehistoric big cats disappeared, leaving only their fangs behind, the local villagers would trek up to this spot bearing the corpses of ancestors they deemed most beneficial. They would shove the bodies deep into the cave, retrieve them after a time, and parade them around while shouting, "They're coming! They're coming!" 

We Malagasy people deeply cherish these secondary funeral rites. We arrange for a live band to arrive by motor vehicle for the occasion. When the bodily decomposition is nearly complete, we embrace our dear departed in our arms once more. Chunks of tissue slide out from the old burial shrouds, dropping much like wet pet food slipping out of a tin. We swaddle the remains in pristine, dry fabric, and their joy brings blessings to our lives. As we carry them through the valley, we offer up specific bones: a finger is left for a deity represented by a raven or a rodent, and a foot bone is buried under the fireplace to bring good fortune. 

And how was good fortune understood? In those days, the realm of the dead lasted a considerable time, though it was neither absurdly endless nor governed by rigid, army-like rules. The spirits of the departed simply came to join the celebration.

Deep within the dramatic contours of our limestone valley lies a hidden cave, shrouded by time and overgrown foliage. For as long as memory serves, this subterranean sanctuary has rested as the final gathering place for our dead. Living in its immediate shadow, our relationship with mortality is not defined by distance or fear, but by an intimate, enduring proximity. 

In our community, death is not viewed as a permanent departure, but as a transitional process honored through the practice of second burials. Years after a loved one is first laid to rest, they are exhumed and brought back into the light of the living. Far from a solemn or somber occasion, this tradition transforms the valley into a place of vibrant celebration. The exhumed ancestors are paraded through the valley, surrounded by joyous music, singing, and the collective memory of the community gathered to honor them once more.

During the central ritual, the physical remains—often partially decayed—are handled with profound tenderness and respect. Relatives gently clean the bones and remaining flesh, stripping away the lingering dirt of the earth to lovingly rewrap their predecessors in layers of fresh, dry linen. This tactile act of care bridges the gap between generations, reassuring the deceased that they remain deeply cherished.

Following the rewrapping, specific body parts are dispersed according to sacred tradition rather than returned entirely to the earth. Certain fragments are carefully placed in distinct locations across the landscape and within the home, such as beneath the domestic hearth. By embedding these physical relics into the spaces of daily life, families secure good fortune and pay homage to the local deities who govern the valley's fortune and fertility.

This rich tapestry of customs is rooted in a unique understanding of the soul's journey. In our tradition, the afterlife is not envisioned as an abstract, eternal void, but rather as a limited, dynamic period. During this fleeting window of existence, the spirits of our ancestors do not merely observe us from afar; they are believed to cross back over, actively joining the living in feast and festival, fully present until their time among us naturally fades.

High above the sun-dappled floor of the valley, carved into the cool limestone cliffs, lies a sanctuary where time seems to stand still. For the villagers living below, this elevated cave is not a place of dread or finality, but a cherished threshold between worlds. Here rest the generation of ancestors who built the homes, tilled the soil, and established the customs that still govern daily life. Every few years, when the season is right, the valley stirs with a distinct kind of anticipation—not for a harvest or a changing of tides, but for the sacred homecoming of the dead.

The practice, rooted in the ancient tradition of secondary burial, is a testament to the belief that love and duty do not end with a person’s last breath. On the morning of the ritual, the village ascends the cliffside path, not in solemn, tearful silence, but accompanied by the warm hum of chatter, music, and shared excitement. Entering the dim, earth-scented mouth of the cave, family members locate the rested remains of their departed relatives. With hands guided by tenderness rather than hesitation, they carefully lift the ancestors from their stone niches and bear them out into the brilliant light of day.

Once gathered on woven bamboo mats in the sunlight, the intimate work begins. The old, weathered shrouds—softened and worn by years in the cave—are gently removed. Relatives clean and perfume the remains, whispering updates about the family while they work, filling the gap of years with news of recent marriages, bumper crops, and newborn children. The ancestors are then bound in fresh, pristine sheets of fine linen, secured with colorful ribbons. Far from being a clinical or morbid task, this rewrapping is an act of deep affection, akin to dressing a loved one for a grand celebration or tucking a child into bed.

With the new shrouds secured, the festival shifts into its most vibrant phase. The ancestors, lifted high on bamboo litters or held close in the arms of their descendants, are carried on a parade through the valley. They are walked past the fields they once plowed, brought to stand before the doors of the homes they once built, and placed in the center of family circles. The air fills with the sounds of traditional instruments, singing, and laughter. Children run alongside the procession, growing up with the understanding that their ancestors are not terrifying ghosts, but beloved guardians who share in their joy.

Through this cyclical act of remembrance, the community profoundly reframes the concept of mortality. In many cultures, death is viewed as an intimidating eternity—a cold, distant abyss that severs ties forever. But here, the afterlife is rendered tangible, warm, and comforting. The ritual strips away the terror of the grave, replacing it with a living, evolving relationship. By physically holding, clothing, and walking with their dead, the living are reminded of their place in a continuous human chain. They leave the festival refreshed, carrying with them the abiding comfort that they walk in the active blessings of their forebears—and that when their own time comes, they too will be tenderly wrapped in fresh linen and brought out to dance in the sun.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of literary fiction that connects a rural English limestone landscape with the Malagasy practice of second burials (Famadihana).
counterfactuals.output:
The limestone did not lie; it remembered being alive. 

Here, high on the bench of Malham Moor, the earth was a hard, pale ribcage protruding through thin turf. Long before the sheep had nibbled it down to the dirt, long before the dry-stone walls were laid like stitches across the hills, this valley had been a warm, shallow sea. Billions of tiny, crinoid sea-lilies and soft-bodied mollusks had died, settled, and crushed into one another, exchanging their soft flesh for calcite, their fleeting lives for enduring white stone.

Solo stood at the breach of a collapsed wall, his breath blossoming into the cold Yorkshire mist. His hands were raw, the knuckles powdered with a fine, chalky dust that sucked the moisture from his skin. In his pocket rested a small bottle of clove oil and a folded square of raw crimson silk—a *lamba mena*—sent by his sister six weeks ago from Antsirabe.

Today was the day. Five thousand miles south, where the soil was the dark, iron-red of a dried scab, his family was gathering. He could hear it in the back of his throat: the shrill, joyful blare of the brass band, the smell of roasted pork and cheap rum, the dull thud of shovels striking the clay as they opened the ancestral vault. They would be pulling his grandfather from the darkness, calling his name into the light, laughing to keep the sadness from curdling into malice.

They would be wrapping the old man’s bones in fresh silk. They would be dancing with him.

Solo picked up a heavy, oblong block of limestone from the fallen rubble. It was cold enough to bite through his thick wool gloves. He set it on his knee, pulled off his gloves with his teeth, and ran his thumb over the pale, weathered grain. Embedded in the center was the unmistakable spiral of an ancient crinoid stem—a tiny, fossilized vertebrae preserved in the rock. A bone of the earth.

In England, the dead were buried once, tucked beneath damp grass, and expected to remain motionless while the centuries stacked above them like slates. It was a cold way to treat an ancestor, Solo thought. To leave them down there in the dark, forgotten, as if death were a quiet room rather than a doorway through which one occasionally returned to party.

He looked around the empty moor. The wind whistled through the grykes—the deep, dark fissures in the limestone pavement behind him—sounding remarkably like a distant horn section. A curlew cried overhead, its sharp, sliding note echoing off the scar.

"Dadabe," Solo whispered. His voice was small against the vast, gray sky, but it was Malagasy, and the limestone seemed to hold it, catching the sibilants in its porous heart.

He took the bottle of clove oil from his coat. He unstoppered it and let three amber drops fall onto the stone. The rich, medicinal heat of the scent flared instantly in the damp air, impossibly alien against the smell of wet bracken and sheep manure. 

He unfolded the crimson silk. The wind tried to snatch it, snapping the delicate fabric like a banner, but Solo caught it, wrapping it securely around the limestone block. The rich red was violently bright against the dull gray of the Dales—a drop of Malagasy sun spilled onto the cold English karst.

He cradled the stone against his chest. It was heavy, sixteen pounds of prehistoric sea-bottom, but he held it as one might hold a child, or a fragile, sleeping old man. 

Slowly, awkwardly, his heavy work boots slipping on the slick grass, Solo began to move. He took three steps to the left, two to the right, swaying his hips in time with a rhythm only he could hear. He spun once, carefully, the wind catching his hair, the crimson-wrapped stone pressed close to his ribcage. He danced. He danced for the sea-lilies that had died three hundred million years ago; he danced for his grandfather, whose wrappings were even now being drenched in perfume under a cloudless highland sky; he danced to remind the cold hill that it, too, had once been warm, wet, and teeming with light.

When he stopped, his lungs were burning. He rested his forehead against the wrapped stone. The cold had bled through the silk, but beneath it, he could imagine a faint, deep warmth—the heat of pressure, of time, of memory preserved.

Solo walked back to the break in the wall. At the foundation, where the ground was firm, he laid the crimson-wrapped limestone down carefully into the gap. He took another stone—rough, heavy, gray—and placed it gently atop the silk, sealing it into the wall. 

It would stay there now. The rain would fall, the silk would slowly fray over decades, the clove oil would fade into the moss, but the stone would remain turned. The bone had been wrapped. The memory had been held.

Solo stood up, dusted the lime from his palms, and picked up his hammer to finish the wall.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a surreal prose poem from the perspective of a narrator living near an ancient cave, reflecting on visceral death rituals, brass bands, and a finite afterlife.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep my cot three yards from the cave’s throat, where the limestone tastes of wet iron and old lard. When a neighbor stops breathing, we do not weep; we peel them like boiled fruit. We scrape the marrow to grease the hinges of the dark, rubbing their knuckles with turmeric and ox-gall until the skin shines like cured sausage. The cave demands a slippery corpse. It likes them rubbed in salt and ground beetle-wings, so they slide easily down the gullet of the karst, past the subterranean aquifers that hum like wet fingers on the rims of a thousand crystal glasses. 

Then come the horns. Not the soft harps of the pious, but a six-man brass procession smelling of stale gin and warm valve oil. They march backward down the damp incline, tubas belching golden, bruised notes into the gloom. The sound is so heavy it vibrates the teeth in our gums—fat, sweating bellies of copper and nickel driving the dead downward with marching polkas and frantic, discordant fanfares. The trombone slides outward, a long metallic tongue licking the dark, shaking the remaining grease from the dead man's heels. We play until the trumpets fill with spit and condensation, blowing the spirit past the point of no echoing.

We do this because down there, eternity is an invention of the sunshine, a lie that rots in the open air. In the damp dark, the afterlife is strictly finite—it has a shelf life no longer than a ham in a cellar. A soul lasts thirty years at best. It wanders the lower galleries, wearing itself thin against the jagged teeth of the rock, shedding its memories like scabbed skin until it is no thicker than a lard-paper wrapper. There is no judgment, only erosion. Slowly, the blare of the brass no longer bounces off the dead; the music passes straight through their translucent ribs, casting no shadow on the wet slate. They thin into steam, settle onto the floor, and calcify into the slow, white icicles that hang from the ceiling. By the time the next funeral band marches down, the old souls are just water dropping onto the bell of a French horn.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dark, slightly humorous vignette in the style of contemporary British experimental fiction about exhuming dead relatives, using vivid and unsettling sensory imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
Tuesday, 08:15. The soil in St. Jude’s overflow plot had the slick, liverish consistency of chilled lard. 

We were digging up Great-Aunt Brenda to make room for a subterranean fiber-optic relay. Mr. Garside, from the Council’s Environmental Health & Exhumations Directorate, stood by the lip of the trench in a high-vis tabard that whistled softly in the drizzle. He was eating a sausage roll from a paper bag, licking flakes of pastry from his thumbs with a small, wet *thwip*.

“Depth of six feet,” Garside muttered, consulting a laminated clipboard. “Though they settle. They always sink toward the mantle. Like currants in a heavy pudding.”

Cousin Nigel lowered the JCB bucket. The engine gave a greasy cough, belching black diesel smoke that settled over the damp nettles. 

When the bucket hit wood, the sound wasn’t a dramatic splintering, but a wet, dense *squelch*—the sound of a heel sinking into a rotten turnip. Thirty-two years of Shropshire rainwater had rendered the mahogany coffin into something resembling soaked Weetabix. 

Nigel hopped down into the pit, his yellow Wellington boots making loud, suction-pop noises in the soup. “Right then,” he said, pulling a pair of Marigold dishwashing gloves over his knuckles. “Let’s get her up before the rain picks up. I’ve got a MOT at ten.”

Sensory inventory of Great-Aunt Brenda, aged eighty-four (at rest since 1991):

1. **Smell:** Not rot, precisely—rot is too lively. It was the heavy, sweetish stench of old damp carpets, boiled cabbage, rancid marzipan, and a sudden, sharp high-note of mothballs.
2. **Visual:** A collapsed accordion of mold-spotted nylon dress (crimson, polka-dot, purchase date unknown). Inside the dress: a greyish, soap-like sludge—*adipocere*, Garside called it, helpfully tapping his clipboard—bonded to fragments of marrow-yellow bone. Her hair remained unnervingly intact, a pristine, static-charged helmet of lavender perm floating atop a deflated skull.
3. **Sound:** The rhythmic *shluck-shluck* of Nigel ladling Brenda’s torso into a heavy-duty rubble sack from B&Q.

“Watch the pelvis, Nige,” I said, leaning over the pit with a thermos of lukewarm Bovril. “You’re slopping her.”

“She’s stuck to the lining,” Nigel grunted. His face was purple from bent-over exertion. He tugged at a handful of rotted lace. *Tear.* “Oh Christ. Her hip’s gone in the silt.”

“Use the trowel,” said Garside, biting off the end of his pastry. “And do mind the dentures. The pink acrylic doesn’t rot. If you leave them behind, the broadband lads’ll find them in the spring and report a murder. Paperwork’s a nightmare.”

Nigel plunged his yellow-gloved hand into the black mud, rummaging with the unbothered focus of a man looking for his keys in a crowded coat pocket. He pulled out a wet, grinning arc of false teeth, plastered in green duckweed.

“Found ‘em,” he panted, wiping them against his thigh. He tossed them into the rubble sack with a dry, ceramic *clatter*. 

We hoisted Brenda out in three separate bags. They clinked and sloshed with the heavy, sodden weight of a wet mattress. We piled her into the boot of Nigel’s Estate, right next to a box of spare fan belts and a bag of half-used lawn feed. 

Nigel peeled off his Marigolds with a rubbery snap. He looked at his watch. 

“Fancy a bacon cob before we take her to the crem?” he asked, wiping a smudge of thirty-year-old silt from his forehead. “I know a van by the B4393. Crisp fat. Proper brown sauce.”

The boot gave a tiny, wet settling sound as the rubble bags shifted in the damp air.

“Go on then,” I said, shivering as a droplet of cold rain slid down the back of my neck. “Make it a double bacon. I’m bloody freezing.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: "We hire a band that comes in a van." Write a flash fiction story around this line that blends paleontology, local landmarks, and ancestral re-wrapping rituals.
counterfactuals.output:
The limestone vault sat beneath the shadow of Dinosaur Ridge, cut directly into the fossil-rich shale of the Morrison Formation. Every seven years, when the scrub oaks on the hogback turned the color of rust, our family gathered to turn the bones.

We didn’t just unwrap our grandmothers; we unwrapped the world that birthed them.

In the vault’s cool darkness lay Great-Aunt Clara, wrapped in deteriorating lace, resting shoulder-to-joint with a three-foot section of an *Allosaurus* tibia our homesteading ancestors had plowed out of the creek bed in 1890. To our line, deep time was simply older lineage. The earth had exhaled them both, so we tendered both.

Grandpa beat the dust from his canvas apron and unrolled bolts of unbleached linen, freshly dyed with red ochre and boiled pine sap. We lifted Clara first, light as dried lavender, humming quietly as we stripped away seven years of damp silt and rotted silk. Next came the heavy, petrified iron of the dinosaur. It took four of us to hoist the fossilized stone-bone onto the cedar table, its marrow long ago replaced by banded agate that caught the thin mountain sunlight.

A party for the dead requires brass, rhythm, and enough bass to rattle the shale. 

We hire a band that comes in a van.

It rolled up the dirt track from the direction of Red Rocks Amphitheatre, a dented ’94 Ford Econoline belching blue exhaust. Five horn players piled out wearing velvet suits that smelled of cloves and diesel. They didn't ask questions about the two-hundred-pound Jurassic femur resting on sawhorses, nor about Clara, who was currently being bound in fresh, fragrant cream-colored shroud-cloth. They simply set up near the ripple-marked dinosaur trackways embedded in the ledge and struck up a slow, swung waltz.

We lifted our kin—both the recent and the primeval—into the afternoon air. 

Cousin Mae danced with Clara, swaying across the bluestem grass, while my brothers and I hefted the agate-heavy vertebra of a *Camarasaurus*, spinning its cool, impossible weight between us. We sprayed lavender water over Clara’s new wraps and brushed linseed oil into the porous, ancient bone to keep the frost from cracking it. 

Under the open sky, a hundred and fifty million years collapsed into the span of a horn solo. We drank cider, spun the wrapped remains of human and sauropod alike, and laid them back down together in the dark, warm earth, ready for their next seven years of sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a creative monologue about how ancient communities handled their dead, contrasting their practical view of the afterlife with modern ideas of eternity.
counterfactuals.output:
*(The speaker sits at a wooden table, gently brushing dust off a centuries-old ceramic shard. They look up, addressing an unseen listener.)*

You moderns have a terrifying relationship with *forever*. 

You seal your dead in heavy steel caskets, vault them in concrete, pump their veins full of chemicals to stop the clock. You act as if decay is a design flaw. You’ve turned eternity into a sterile, endless waiting room—a static white void where souls float around like dust motes in a shaft of light, doing… what, exactly? Nothing. Just existing. Forever.

Gods, it sounds exhausting.

The ancients… they knew better. They didn’t deal in abstract infinitives. They were practical people, and they treated death like what it actually was: a relocation. A chore. A journey that required proper packing.

When a Bronze Age village laid a hunter in the earth, they didn’t weep for his "immortal soul" in some ethereal heavens. They put a copper dagger in his hand, a leather pouch of dried meat at his belt, and a pair of sturdy leather boots on his feet. Why? Because the road past the horizon was long, and it was rocky, and a man without boots is an idiot, living or dead.

They buried their women with loom weights, their children with little clay rattles, their kings with chariots and brewing vats. Death wasn't an exit from reality; it was an extension of the local economy! You paid Charon his coin because ferrying a boat takes labor. You poured honey into the dirt because the dead get thirsty, and a thirsty ancestor is a cranky ancestor. 

The afterlife wasn't a reward or a punishment. It was a landscape. It had rivers you had to ford, gatekeepers you had to bribe, and fields that needed harvesting. The dead were busy! They were guarding the sheep from spirit-wolves, or guiding the rainclouds over the summer wheat. 

They didn't want *eternity*. They wanted *continuity*. 

To them, the dead weren't gone—they were just in the lower pasture. They were in the soil, in the stone of the hearth, in the marrow of the oak tree. The body decayed, yes, but that rot was a gift! It was the flesh paying its rent back to the earth that had fed it for fifty years. To deny the worms was to rob the garden.

And now? Look at us. We are so terrified of being forgotten, so obsessed with preserving the vessel, that we’ve made death lonely. We hide it in sterile hospital rooms behind pale blue curtains. We trade the rich, dark loam of memory for chiseled granite that says nothing except a name and two dates. We’ve traded a bustling, working spirit-world for a cold, terrifying infinity.

*(The speaker sets down the pottery shard and looks directly at the listener, leaning in slightly.)*

When my time comes, don't put me in a vault. Don't fight the earth on my behalf. 

Just give me a pair of good shoes, a cup of strong wine, and brush the dirt over my face. I don't need your endless, empty eternity. I have a long walk ahead of me... and I intend to be useful.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
